concurrency_model.participants: 100 worker goroutines plus the caller goroutine
concurrency_model.shared_output: one io.Writer, but only the token holder writes
concurrency_model.ordering_invariant: worker i+1 cannot write before it receives worker i's token; worker i sends only after its write and error report
concurrency_model.synchronization: unbuffered channel rendezvous for every predecessor/successor edge
concurrency_model.termination: caller receives token[100] only after every worker has completed its finite path

liveness_review.write_error_path: pass; errors are buffered so a returned writer error does not prevent token handoff
liveness_review.blocking_writer_boundary: explicitly out of contract; a forever-blocking Writer would stop the chain and requires a new cancellation/timeout contract

findings: The raw interview note places the problem immediately after Go GMP/goroutine scheduling questions, so Go goroutines are source-supported rather than inferred from generic coroutine terminology.
The candidate does not claim that the source requires channels; channel token passing is explicitly a solution choice.
Each write is sequenced before the worker's token send, and the corresponding channel communication synchronizes predecessor and successor, yielding a transitive ordering proof for 1..100.
No two workers can reach the Writer concurrently because possession of the token is exclusive along the chain; the race-enabled fixture also reports no race.
The final-token wait makes normal worker lifetimes explicit. A Writer that never returns is correctly documented as a separate cancellation boundary rather than hidden.

The generic repository Coding standard asks for Java, but this Canonical is explicitly Go-specific. Adding Java would not demonstrate goroutine semantics; the source-language Go implementation is retained and the conflict remains visible for human pilot review.
